title: How wide a UTF-8 code point gets
prompt:
UTF-8 as standardized today (RFC 3629; Unicode code points run to U+10FFFF). A code point is encoded as a variable number of bytes.

What is the largest number of bytes UTF-8 ever uses for a single code point?

Type the number only.
reveal:
4.

  code points          bytes
  U+0000 - U+007F      1      ASCII, byte-for-byte identical
  U+0080 - U+07FF      2      Latin-1 supplement, Greek, Cyrillic, Hebrew, Arabic
  U+0800 - U+FFFF      3      the rest of the BMP, most CJK included
  U+10000 - U+10FFFF   4      emoji, historic scripts, rare CJK

The original 1993 design ran to 6 bytes; RFC 3629 cut it to 4 when Unicode capped itself at U+10FFFF.

The practical consequence is that bytes, code points, and characters-a-user-sees are three different counts: a buffer or a VARCHAR sized in bytes is not sized in characters, and truncating a byte string at a fixed offset can split a code point in half. UTF-16 has its own version of the trap - a Java char and a JavaScript string index are UTF-16 code units, so an astral code point such as U+1F680 takes two of them: that one-character string has length 2 in Java and JavaScript, and 1 in Python 3.
